question: how exactly is altitude calculated airplanes?
answer: i feel like there's a lot of confusing information in this thread. let me bullet point the truths: * modern aircraft use gps. * all aircraft (including said modern ones, technically their primary readout!) use a reading of outside air pressure to determine altitude. atc and automated stations at airports broadcast local air pressure so the altimeters can be calibrated to the navigation charts along the route. * when you land in denver, **the altimeter reads 5000**. the navigation charts mark the airfield (and other navigation aids/obstacles) at their actual altitude. fun fact: there is another metric called "density altitude" which pilots use to gauge aircraft performance. on a hot day when the air is less dense, an airfield normally at 5000' can "behave" like it's at a much higher altitude, meaning you need a longer runway to take off among other things. this is one of many reasons why mountain flying can be treacherous sometimes! source: me, pilot
